frames.narration: A customer adds a pen to a shopping cart. The application sends a put with the cart's key, the new cart and the context it got from its earlier read. The context holds the cart's vector clock, so the store knows which version this update builds on.

The coordinator hashes the key with MD5 to a position on the ring and finds its preference list: the nodes that follow that position clockwise, B, C and D, with spares behind them. Every node can work this out for itself, so the request went straight here without being routed through other nodes.

states.coordinator: key -> position -> nodes B, C, D

frames.narration: The coordinator writes the new version locally with a new vector clock and sends it to the nodes of the preference list. Node D cannot be reached. A strict quorum would now fail or lose durability. Dynamo uses a sloppy quorum: it takes the first N healthy nodes in the list instead, so the copy meant for D goes to node E.

messages.label: copy meant for D, with a hint

frames.narration: With the usual (N, R, W) of (3, 2, 2), the write needs two acknowledgements. B and C answer, so the coordinator reports success. The customer's add-to-cart was accepted even though one of the three nodes was down.

Meanwhile another browser tab, working from the old cart, added a mug through a different coordinator. Now there are two versions with vector clocks that neither descends from the other. A later get asks the replicas, waits for R = 2 answers, and finds both.

Dynamo does not guess. It returns both versions to the application along with a context that summarises their clocks. The application knows what a cart is, so it merges them into one cart with both the pen and the mug, and writes that back with the context, which collapses the two branches into a single new version. No add-to-cart is lost, though an item the customer had deleted could reappear.

Later node D comes back. E, which has been holding the hinted replica in a separate local store and checking on D, delivers it and deletes its own copy, so the number of replicas never dropped. After the read, the coordinator also updates any replica that gave a stale answer, which is called read repair.

In the background, replicas that share a key range compare Merkle trees. If the root hashes match, the data matches and nothing is sent. If they differ, they compare child hashes and descend only into the branches that differ, so only the keys that are really out of step are transferred. This catches differences that hints and read repair missed.
